summary:
THE WAY BACK HOME is an interactive and adventurous game aimed at teaching children about space sciences through story-based game mechanics. It was created within 48 hours as part of the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

The plot of the game revolves around a crewed NASA mission to Mars that ends up being in trouble because the vehicle crashes on the planet and leaves the astronauts stranded there. In order to make their way back home, the players need to explore the area, find some equipment left behind by NASA in the course of previous missions to Mars and use the components to fix the spaceship.

The game solves the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten" since it turns the abandoned technologies left behind by NASA in the course of its exploration missions to Mars into interactive and engaging elements of a learning process.

The overall idea of our game is to make the scientific education fun and interesting for the players.
details:
1. What does it do & how does it work?
The Long Way Home is an interactive, two-chapter 2D pixel-art survival and space-science adventure game that runs directly in the browser. You play as a stranded astronaut whose Ares IV spacecraft crash-landed on Mars. Instead of reading a textbook about space exploration, players live through real NASA engineering challenges to rebuild their ship and make it back to Earth:
Top-Down Survival & Exploration: Players walk around a 56×38-tile planetary map (using keyboard WASD/Arrows, click-to-walk, or mobile touch controls) while managing Suit Oxygen and Suit Power reserves. Leaving the spacecraft's blue life-support safe zone drains resources—especially during Martian dust storms—teaching resource management and risk-reward planning.
Chapter 1 — Mars (Rebuilding Ares IV & Finding Earth):
Mars Pathfinder Airbag Run: Players meet the 1997 Mars Pathfinder rover and play a fast-paced side-scrolling canyon runner to collect 10 inflatable Airbags, restoring the rocket's landing cushioning.
Blind Landing (Ingenuity Mars Helicopter): Players interact with the Ingenuity helicopter relay and solve a 3-sector grid-programming puzzle. Because radio signals between Earth and Mars have a multi-minute delay, players must pre-program an entire waypoint flight path within a battery budget to recover 3 Steel Alloys for outer plating.
Kepler Space Telescope (Locate Earth): Once the rocket is 100% repaired, players run an onboard Kepler transit photometry scan. Across three levels (Hot Jupiter, Neptune-size, and Earth!), they spot repeating brightness dips in star light curves—and use a 9-point moving-average noise filter ("Clean up noise") to uncover Earth's tiny signal buried in sensor noise.
Chapter 2 — The Moon (Emergency Detour & Return Home):
After a mid-flight detour forces an emergency landing on the Moon, players scavenge 4 Plutonium-238 cores from historic Apollo wreckage sites, load them into a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) to convert radioactive decay heat into electricity, charge a Lunar Rover, drive 900m across physics-driven lunar craters and low-gravity hills to Lunar Fuel Base 02 for cryogenic rocket fuel, and finally launch home to Earth.
2. What benefits does it have?
Learn by Doing, Not Memorizing: Abstract STEM concepts—like radio communication latency, exoplanet transit photometry, signal-to-noise filtering, radioisotope thermoelectric power, and low-gravity rover physics—are transformed into intuitive, playable mechanics.
Bite-Sized Scientific Storytelling: Before each minigame, an animated astronaut dialogue modal shares real historical milestones (e.g., Pathfinder bouncing ~15 times on Mars on July 4, 1997; Ingenuity's 2,500+ RPM coaxial rotors in Mars's 1% atmosphere; Kepler's 84-parts-per-million Earth transit dip) in short, digestible lines with retro typewriter audio blips.
Accessible & Zero-Barrier: Runs in any modern desktop or mobile browser with keyboard, mouse click-to-move, and on-screen touch controls, plus automatic localStorage saving so kids can pause and resume anytime.
Safe Failure & Practice Modes: Players can replay minigames in Practice Mode, retry failed sectors immediately, or respawn at the Lunar Landing Pad if oxygen runs out—encouraging experimentation and resilience rather than frustration.
3. What is the intended impact of the project?
The goal is to spark curiosity in space exploration, astronomy, and engineering for younger learners and students by showing why spacecraft are designed the way they are:
Instead of just knowing "Mars has rovers and helicopters," kids understand how engineers solve impossible constraints (e.g., Why use airbags to bounce on Mars? Why can't we fly a Mars helicopter with a live joystick? How do scientists find an Earth-sized planet around a bright star when the signal is noisy?).
It turns players into active problem-solvers—connecting physics, coding/logic (command queuing), data analysis (reading light curves), and history (Apollo, Pathfinder, Kepler, Ingenuity) into one cohesive journey home.
4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?
Languages & Core Stack: TypeScript and React 19 bundled with Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS v4 and Motion (motion/react) for smooth UI transitions and dialogue animations, plus Lucide React icons.
Custom 2D Rendering & Physics: Built from scratch using the HTML5 Canvas 2D API—including a custom pixel-art planetary renderer (pixelRenderer.ts), a custom 8-bit procedural finale cutscene renderer (earthReturnRenderer.ts), custom pixel-art SVG models (astronaut, Ingenuity, Kepler), particle systems (engine smoke, dust, sparks), and custom 2D rover suspension/terrain physics.
Procedural Audio Engine: Built with the browser's Web Audio API (audio.ts and cutsceneAudio.ts)—synthesizing retro footsteps, dialogue blips, alerts, and an original 8-bit chiptune soundtrack with zero external audio-file dependencies.
Multimedia & Persistence: Pre-rendered MP4 story cutscenes for Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 transitions, alongside browser localStorage state persistence (saveSystem.ts).
Hardware: Standard consumer laptop/desktop browser environment (runs smoothly at 60fps on any computer, tablet, or smartphone without requiring a dedicated GPU or backend server).
5. How is your project creative?
Genre-Hopping Gameplay Unified by Story: Each real-world NASA technology gets its own distinct game genre that mirrors how that technology actually works—an endless canyon jumper for Pathfinder's bouncing airbags, a blind command-queue puzzle for Ingenuity's signal-delayed autopilot, a scientific light-curve detector for Kepler, and a hill-climbing physics racer for the Lunar Rover.
Authentic Data Science Disguised as a Puzzle: In the Find Earth minigame, kids literally apply a 9-point centered moving average to Gaussian noise over a 300-point brightness graph—seeing firsthand how data smoothing reveals hidden planetary transits.
Custom Retro Aesthetics & Procedural Chiptune Finale: Rather than relying on generic templates, the world features hand-crafted pixel-art sprites, glowing hazard rings, Martian dust storms, and a multi-scene animated 8-bit victory sequence ("Cosmo Boy: The Unlikely Return") synchronized to synthesized Web Audio music.
6. What factors did your team consider?
Balancing Education with Fun (Pacing & Retention): We avoided walls of text. Scientific explanations are delivered through short, character-driven dialogue lines right before the player uses that exact concept in a fun minigame—creating an immediate "Aha!" connection.
Guided Navigation for Young Players: Large maps can overwhelm younger players, so we built a Tactical Map (G), an optional Radar Minimap (Tab), compass bearings with meter distances, and a one-click auto-walk-to-objective feature so players never get lost.
Performance & Cross-Device Usability: The 60fps canvas loop automatically pauses during video cutscenes so playback never stutters, canvas zoom adapts dynamically to screen width, and mobile players get dedicated TouchControls alongside desktop keyboard/mouse controls.
Clear Visual Feedback & Safety: The blue life-support safe zone around the rocket gives instant visual relief when recharging oxygen/power, warning hints pop up cleanly on context, and localStorage autosaves every 2 seconds so accidental refreshes never erase a kid's progress.
